Issued at 413 AM CDT Sat Aug 22 2026

A highly-amplified upper level wave pattern lies over North 
America early this morning, with a ridge axis along the Rockies
and a trough axis from Hudson Bay to the Southern Appalachian 
Mountains. Surface high pressure is centered over southeast 
Saskatchewan, which is keeping the local weather very quiet. 
The surface high will morph into an elongated ridge and slide 
over the Red River Valley by the end of the day as the upper 
ridge axis begins to pivot off the Northern Rockies. Quiet 
weather will continue through the daytime hours, with high 
temperatures this afternoon ranging from the mid 70s northeast 
to mid 80s southwest.

A mid level shortwave will eject off the Northern Rockies by 
this evening, cutting through the ridge axis. The increasing 
downstream warm-air advection, moisture transport, isentropic 
lift, etc. could generate showers and thunderstorms in eastern 
Montana tonight, spreading into western North Dakota early 
Sunday morning. MUCAPE could exceed 1000 J/kg with effective 
bulk shear near 30 kts in the southwest Sunday morning, but 
convection should remain elevated, and most CAMs are only 
simulating scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms. The 
00Z NAMnest is an outlier with a couple of clusters of strong 
to severe storms with bowing segments in the southwest Sunday 
morning and into the afternoon. Proximity model soundings at 
Dickinson do show higher RH at the base of the EML and higher 
equilibrium levels in the NAMnest, but its hodographs could 
best be described as chaotic. Therefore, the risk for severe 
weather Sunday morning into the early afternoon is very low, 
but not zero. This could change later Sunday afternoon as 
diurnal heating opens the potential for surface or mixed-layer 
based convection. However: 1) there is high confidence in a 
strong capping inversion above the boundary layer, 2) a moist 
southeasterly surface flow is not conducive to efficient 
boundary layer mixing, and 3) mid level clouds and/or anvil 
shading from morning convection could limit diurnal heating to 
some extent. CAMs do show an increased probability in stronger 
convection over south central North Dakota mid to late Sunday 
afternoon along the eastern gradient of the buoyancy pool, 
where CIN may be relatively weaker. Still looking at a CAPE/ 
shear parameter space supportive of only marginally severe 
storms though. But regardless of intensity, there are still 
medium chances (30 to 60 percent) for showers and thunderstorms
across much of western and central North Dakota Sunday 
afternoon and evening as the shortwave moves through. Increased 
confidence in the aforementioned southeasterly flow and cloud 
cover has cooled the high temperature forecast into the lower 
and mid 80s for all but far southwest North Dakota on Sunday.

By Sunday night, a much more potent shortwave/upper low will be
ejecting off the Canadian Rockies into the southern prairie 
provinces. Clusters of thunderstorms forming off the Montana 
Rockies late Sunday afternoon could cross into western North 
Dakota Sunday night before dissipating. If this convection is 
maintained, it could be strong to severe as it moves into a 
higher buoyancy air mass with increasing shear. The 06Z HRRR 
appears to show a reasonable worst-case scenario with a broken 
line of strong to severe storms extending from the Canadian to 
South Dakota borders entering the state after 10 PM CDT. 
Simulated surface winds gusts in the 06Z HRRR are much lower in
western North Dakota though than they are in eastern Montana 
earlier in the evening. 

The thunderstorm forecast on Monday remains uncertain and may 
end up highly dependent on the eastward propagation of the 
occluded front attendant to the potent Canadian upper low. Both 
CAPE (~2000 J/kg) and shear (~35 kts) directly ahead of the 
front are projected to be sufficient for severe storms. But very
few ensemble members are generating any convection along the 
front, likely due to an absence of mid to upper level forcing. 
Broad mid level height falls do eventually spread into northern 
North Dakota, but that may lag behind the surface front. The 
latest NBM has reduced PoPs to only 20 to 30 percent Monday 
afternoon and evening, and kept mentionable PoPs east of Highway
83. But location uncertainty in the surface front at 00Z Monday
evening ranges from as far west as Minot to Dickinson (NAM) to 
as far east as Devils Lake to Jamestown (a small subset of GEFS 
members). The progression of the front is also likely to play a 
role in high temperatures on Monday. Strong mixing in the dry 
post-frontal air mass could allow temperatures to approach 90 
in southwest and south central North Dakota, with at least 
lower 80s elsewhere. This is assuming a slightly quicker 
frontal progression, which ensembles do tilt towards.

Ensemble guidance shows the Canadian low digging southeastward 
on Tuesday, but with variance in its trajectory. That
